item.title: China welcomes more countries to explore pathways for AI capacity-building cooperation: spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
China welcomes more countries to explore pathways for AI capacity-building cooperation: spokesperson BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- China welcomes more countries to join the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, explore more pathways for international cooperation on AI capacity-building, and promote global artificial intelligence (AI) development for good and for all with concrete actions, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday. Guo made the remarks at a regular news briefing when asked to comment on China's Progress Report on the AI Capacity-Building Action Plan for Good and for All, released at the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan), and China's views on the role of AI capacity-building in global governance. Guo said that AI is an emerging field in global governance, and a litmus test for the effectiveness of the global governance system. "The global governance system would not become more just and equitable without the collective capacity enhancement of the Global South, and requires concrete efforts to strengthen the representation and voice of developing countries," he said. Guo said China advocates for respecting the digital sovereignty of all countries. "We believe that every country has the right to possess the foundational capabilities for independent AI development, and to seek a development path suited to its national conditions and practical needs, one that enables AI to be applied in real-world scenarios, address real problems, and generate sustained value," Guo added. item.title: Displaced residents moving into prefab homes three days after Xizang quake
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
Displaced residents moving into prefab homes three days after Xizang quake A drone photo taken on Oct. 26, 2026 shows prefabricated houses at a resettlement site of a quake-hit village in Maru Township of Baqen County, Nagqu City, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Gaesang Namgyae) BAQEN, Xizang, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Three days after the 7.0-magnitude earthquake damaged his home, Tsewang Khangshi was busy moving folding beds and quilts into his temporary new home. On Sunday, the 36-year-old villager from Baqen County moved from a tent to a prefabricated house, which rescue workers had rushed against the clock to build in the wake of the quake that struck on Oct. 22, killing 16 people and injuring 76 others. More than 12,000 residents were evacuated, and 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds were damaged or destroyed, according to local authorities. Baqen County in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, the epicenter of the earthquake, perches at an altitude of nearly 4,800 meters. Tiding over the cold winter has been a top concern for displaced residents like Tsewang Khangshi. Large quantities of disaster relief supplies had arrived in the disaster zone in batches. As of 11 a.m. on Oct. 24, 52,450 items or sets of disaster relief supplies had been sent to the quake zone, including 4,651 tents, 2,000 prefabricated houses, 11,772 folding beds, 5,715 quilts and other cold-weather necessities. Within five hours of the earthquake, the first tents had been erected. All affected residents, including Tsewang Khangshi's family, had moved into temporary tent shelters by Oct. 23. His family moved into a prefabricated house on Oct. 25. "We are so happy we can move into a prefabricated house," he said, packing quilts, clothes and folding beds into his vehicle -- all relief supplies delivered in the immediate aftermath of the quake. The high altitude, low temperatures and strong winds have posed challenges for both residents and rescue workers. Gusts reached up to 13 meters per second, making it difficult to keep warm, particularly at night. To provide better protection against the harsh weather, construction teams and power workers have worked around the clock to build sturdier, warmer temporary homes. The first 60 prefabricated housing units in the earthquake zone were completed at 2:10 a.m. on Oct. 25, and electricity was connected to the units by 8 p.m. on the same day. "We will ensure that affected residents have safe shelter, warm clothing and bedding, hot meals and clean drinking water," said Pan Zhiqing, Party chief of the Nagqu Municipal Emergency Management Bureau. "As more prefabricated units are completed, we will gradually move residents out of tents and into better-heated housing." As the new housing units became available, families began moving in, cleaning their rooms and arranging furniture. The sound of people carrying belongings and chatting filled the settlement in the afternoon sunshine. Outside, workers went from door to door, checking electrical wiring and the sealing of windows and doors against drafts. "All the prefabricated houses are fitted with chimneys for stove use, and we must ensure residents can stay warm through the winter," said Zhang Xuhui, a construction team leader with China Railway. item.title: China sees steady growth in domestic tourism over first 9 months of 2026
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
China sees steady growth in domestic tourism over first 9 months of 2026 BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- China's domestic tourism market posted solid growth in terms of both trips and travel spending from January to September this year, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism (MCT) said on Monday. More than 5.3 billion domestic trips were made during the first nine months of 2026, up 6.2 percent year on year, data from a survey of domestic travelers conducted by the ministry revealed. Urban residents accounted for over 4 billion trips, an increase of 6.6 percent from a year earlier, while rural residents made 1.27 billion trips, marking a 5.1-percent rise. Domestic tourism spending expanded 2.2 percent year on year to 4.95 trillion yuan (about 737 billion U.S. dollars) during these nine months. Of the total, urban residents spent 4.14 trillion yuan, up 2.2 percent, while rural residents spent 810 billion yuan, rising 2.1 percent. China aims to record 8.3 billion year-round domestic trips and 7.7 trillion yuan in year-round domestic travel spending by 2030, according to a five-year tourism development plan for the 2026-2030 period released by the MCT in July. In 2025, the country saw more than 6.5 billion domestic trips, with tourism expenditure reaching 6.3 trillion yuan, both setting new records. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. item.title: Explainer: How a ruling party rules itself -- CPC's perspective
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
Explainer: How a ruling party rules itself -- CPC's perspective This photo taken on March 11, 2026 shows the Great Hall of the People, the venue for the closing meeting of the fourth session of the 14th National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), in Beijing, capital of China. (Xinhua/Wang Xi) BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- With more than 100 million members and the responsibility of governing a country of over 1.4 billion people, the Communist Party of China (CPC) faces an enduring task: identifying and addressing issues within its own ranks. The task has taken on fresh relevance as the CPC prepares to convene the fifth plenary session of its 20th Central Committee in Beijing on Monday. The four-day meeting is scheduled to deliberate on a draft decision on several major issues on persistently advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance. As Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has pointed out, the CPC's full and rigorous self-governance is a great practice in the Party's self-reform in the new era, and has created a new frontier in its self-reform. WHY PERSISTENT SELF-REFORM? At a gathering marking the CPC's 105th founding anniversary in July, Xi said the Party focuses on self-strengthening and always brims with vigor and vitality, referring to it as one of its fine qualities with no parallel among other political parties and political forces. In its pursuit of a better life for the Chinese people, the Party has addressed development challenges through comprehensively deepening reform, while pursuing self-reform to enhance its governing capacity. Since the reform and opening-up in 1978, China has undergone profound transformations. Having achieved tremendous success from humble beginnings, reform efforts have now entered a "deep-water zone." Xi once compared the remaining difficult reforms as "tough bones that are hard to chew." As reforms have advanced into more complex stages, the CPC views full and rigorous governance of the Party as an essential guarantee. Under the banner of self-reform, the CPC has made persistent efforts to improve Party conduct, build a clean government and fight corruption. Haris Bilal Malik, a research fellow at the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad in Pakistan, said the CPC's approach treated self-reform as a continuing responsibility of the governing organization. Internal inspections, disciplinary supervision and anti-corruption measures were intended to identify organizational weaknesses, enforce standards of conduct and strengthen policy implementation, he said. Members of Communist Party of China (CPC) review the Party admission oath beside the replica of a boat, now referred to as the Red Boat, on which CPC founders concluded their meeting in 1921, on Nanhu Lake in Jiaxing, east China's Zhejiang Province, June 30, 2025. (Xinhua/Xu Yu) Helga Zepp-LaRouche, founder and president of the Schiller Institute, linked the CPC's concept of self-reform to the Confucian tradition of lifelong learning and self-improvement. She said improving governance capacity required a political culture within the Party that was oriented toward serving the people. Volker Tschapke, honorary president of Germany's Prussian Society, said the CPC's efforts went beyond short-term campaigns, reflecting a commitment to continuous self-examination. "This is not for show, this is character," he told Xinhua. HOW DOES OVERSIGHT BECOME ROUTINE? A central question is how self-reform efforts can bring about lasting changes in how officials and institutions operate. The central Party leadership's eight-point decision on improving work conduct, adopted in December 2012, set out rules governing research tours, meetings, documentation and other official duties. Its implementation has targeted problems ranging from the misuse of public funds for holiday gifts to misconduct outside working hours, with regulations, inspections and disciplinary measures reinforcing compliance. Anti-corruption efforts have also continued. China's top anti-graft authorities filed cases against 181 officials directly administered by the Organization Department of the Central Committee of the CPC in 2025, according to the work report of the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The work report also revealed that discipline inspection and supervisory authorities filed more than 1 million cases in 2025 and placed 47,000 individuals under detention. A total of 983,000 people received Party disciplinary or administrative punishment. Some 26,000 individuals voluntarily surrendered. Pavel Troshchinsky, a lead researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences' Institute of China and Contemporary Asia, said China's anti-corruption efforts had moved from "paper requirements" to "real action." He highlighted the CPC's emphasis on ensuring that officials dare not, cannot and will not engage in corruption, combining punishment, institutional restraints and stronger ethical awareness. The CPC has also institutionalized regular inspections to assess whether Party organizations are implementing central decisions, exercising power properly and fulfilling their responsibilities. Inspection teams identify problems and provide feedback, while the organizations concerned must take corrective action under follow-up supervision. In 2025, the fifth and sixth rounds of inspections under the 20th CPC Central Committee were carried out in succession, completing full coverage of all provincial-level regions. The emphasis on corrective action can also be seen in China's environmental governance. Central environmental inspections examine whether local Party committees and governments are fulfilling their environmental protection responsibilities. Following the first round of inspections, which covered all 31 provincial-level regions by the end of 2017, inspection teams conducted a major follow-up review in 2018, covering 20 regions in two batches. Regulations issued in 2025 also provide for follow-up reviews of corrective action when necessary. In south China's Guangdong Province, inspectors found in 2018 that efforts to tackle pollution in the Lianjiang River had made insufficient progress. The findings prompted local authorities to accelerate wastewater treatment projects and tighten controls on industrial discharges. The river's water quality has since improved through sustained cleanup efforts. HOW DOES DISCIPLINE SHAPE DEVELOPMENT? A farmer shows an edible fungus cultivated with the Juncao technology at Yuanyi Village of Minning Town, Yongning County of Yinchuan, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, Sept. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Yang Zhisen) The effects of discipline and oversight extend beyond official conduct to the management of public resources and the implementation of development policies. Efforts to tackle corruption and misconduct in school meal programs offer an example. In 2025, disciplinary and supervisory authorities across China handled 61,000 cases involving corruption and misconduct in such programs, with 35,000 people receiving Party disciplinary or administrative sanctions, according to a report published in February 2026. The authorities also pushed for tighter oversight of school meal funds, procurement and food safety. Waleed Gaballah, a member of the Egyptian Association for Political Economy, Statistics and Legislation, said full and rigorous Party self-governance could strengthen fiscal discipline by curbing the misuse of public funds, reducing waste and improving the implementation of development projects. Emmanuel Matambo, research director of the Center for Africa-China Studies at the University of Johannesburg, said China's experience highlighted the importance of combining development commitments with the ability to recognize shortcomings and correct mistakes. Drawing on China's economic transformation and poverty reduction achievements, he emphasized that governing parties must ensure their policies deliver tangible benefits to the public. Tschapke drew on his visits to China to describe the changes he had witnessed in rural communities and infrastructure. "I have seen with my own eyes what has been achieved: how villages have blossomed through targeted poverty alleviation, how rural areas have found new hope, how high-speed rail connects people and hearts," he said. He associated those changes with the CPC's emphasis on public welfare and its efforts to ensure that resources reach the grassroots. Ruslan Yesin, head of the Department of Comprehensive Chinese Studies at Belarusian State University, attributed the CPC's governance achievements to its combination of long-term planning and pragmatic implementation, commitment to mutually beneficial international cooperation, and people-centered approach to development. Yesin said China's experience offers valuable lessons for the Global South in sustaining steady growth, improving livelihoods and enhancing the capacity for independent development. item.title: Xi leads CPC to advance full, rigorous self-governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
Xi leads CPC to advance full, rigorous self-governance BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee on Monday started a four-day plenary session in Beijing, which focuses on strengthening Party self-governance. This marks the latest move by the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core to strengthen the Party through full and rigorous self-governance. Xi, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has emphasized that exercising full and rigorous self-governance is an enduring task for the Party. "One has to be very strong if he wants to strike the iron," Xi said shortly after his election to the post of general secretary of the CPC Central Committee in November 2012. He later warned at a group study session of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee that if corruption is allowed to grow unchecked, "it could spell the end of both the Party and the state." As China entered the new era, the CPC, the largest governing party in the world, faced unprecedented challenges in ensuring reform, development and stability, and addressing problems and risks confronting the nation. Xi has stressed that China's success hinges on the Party, and has made clear that the CPC must continuously strengthen itself through self-governance. In 2014, he explicitly put forward the concept of "exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance" as part of the Party's four-pronged governing strategy, alongside building a moderately prosperous society in all respects, deepening reform and advancing law-based governance. He has made full and rigorous Party self-governance a long-term strategy, as he considers it vital to the Party's long-term governance, the country's enduring stability, and the people's happiness and well-being. BREAK NEW GROUND In December 2012, Xi began strengthening Party self-governance by introducing a code of conduct that became known as the "eight-point rules." It established regulations for Party leaders regarding research tours, meetings, documentation, and other official duties, cracking down on lavish banquets, red carpet events, pomp, entourages, unnecessary meetings, and luxury perks that had once been regarded by some as typical symbols of power. Its implementation has helped curb longstanding malpractices, with effects extending beyond Party and government offices to wider society. "The eight-point rules have indeed brought about fundamental changes over the years," Xi said last year, when the Party launched a campaign to reinforce this code of conduct and consolidate the improvements it had brought about. Xi also launched an unprecedented anti-corruption storm that has swept every corner of public office, netting both high-ranking "tigers" and lower-level "flies." Some of the most senior officials -- including former members of the Political Bureau and its Standing Committee, top military brass, and retirees who left their leading positions years ago -- have been brought to justice. The anti-corruption campaign has continued unabated, with Xi stressing that the fight is an ongoing endeavor. In 2025 alone, 115 officials at ministerial level or above were placed under investigation, while 627,000 people were disciplined in cases involving misconduct and corruption that affect the people's immediate interests. The same year, China also opened investigations into more than 500 cases of cross-border corruption. At a plenary session of the CPC's top disciplinary body early this year, Xi again warned that corruption remains a problem that arises all too easily and frequently. "We must see the fight against corruption through to the end, no matter how great the resistance or how high the cost," he said. "No one who engages in corruption will be shown leniency, regardless of who they are, how high their rank or how great their contributions." EFFECTIVE APPROACHES To strengthen full and rigorous Party self-governance, it is imperative to uphold the Party's overall leadership. Over the past 14 years, the Party's leadership has been further affirmed in both the Party Constitution and the country's Constitution. Central commissions have been established to oversee key areas including reform, national security, cyberspace affairs, and financial and economic affairs. Working mechanisms for central decision-making and coordinating bodies have also been strengthened. Strengthening theoretical education is another approach. With Xi at the helm, the CPC has launched nine Party-wide major education campaigns. The latest one, launched in February this year, prodded Party members to fix their mindset regarding governance performance, aiming to stamp out the tendency among some officials to sacrifice public well-being in seeking to polish their performance records. This campaign built on the gains of previous ones on Party discipline and implementing the eight-point rules, among others, to advance the Party's self-governance. These efforts have gone hand in hand with institution-building. Under Xi's watch, the Party and state oversight systems have been improved. The National Commission of Supervision and local supervisory commissions were established to bring everyone in public office, regardless of Party membership, under supervision. And Xi has made discipline inspections a key instrument of intra-Party oversight. The inspection system allows higher-level Party authorities to send teams to examine how officials exercise power and carry out the central leadership's policies. Inspectors interview officials and members of the public, review documents and receive complaints. They report their findings to Party authorities. After each round of inspections launched by the Party Central Committee, Xi reviewed the reports in detail, assessed the problems uncovered and pushed for further improvements in inspection work. Since 2012, the Party has also formulated or revised an unprecedented number of internal regulations, building a comprehensive framework of rules to confine power in "a cage of institutions." Noting the progress, Xi also warned that in some localities, rules were poorly enforced while "hidden rules" prevailed. He stressed that regulations must become "high-voltage lines" and that power must be exercised transparently, leaving no room for such hidden rules. All these mechanisms are part of the integrated efforts to ensure officials, in Xi's words, "do not have the audacity, opportunity, or desire to become corrupt." LEADING MODERNIZATION DRIVE Full and rigorous Party self-governance serves a broader purpose: strengthening the Party's capacity to lead China's modernization drive. "To successfully achieve the goals and tasks of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), it is imperative to focus on enhancing the ability and competence of the Party in leading economic and social development," Xi told senior provincial- and ministerial-level officials attending a study session at the Party School of the CPC Central Committee earlier this year. He urged Party officials to become more capable of pursuing high-quality development, serving the people, and guarding against and defusing risks. China has entered a critical period for achieving the goal of basically realizing modernization by 2035, and still faces rising uncertainty abroad and mounting challenges at home. At such critical junctures, strong Party leadership is vital to chart the course. All Party members, Xi said, must remain true to the Party's original aspiration and mission, and lead the nation to "create new historic glories." Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: China marks anniversary of Taiwan's recovery with events across Taiwan Strait
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
China marks anniversary of Taiwan's recovery with events across Taiwan Strait This photo shows a commemorative stamp issued by China Post to mark Taiwan Recovery Day. China Post issued a commemorative stamp marking Taiwan Recovery Day on Sunday. Featuring the Great Wall, Alishan and Sun Moon Lake, the stamp attracted strong interest from collectors at postal outlets and online platforms across the mainland. (Xinhua) BEIJING/TAIPEI, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- China on Sunday marked the 81st anniversary of its recovery of Taiwan and observed Taiwan Recovery Day, with commemorative events held across the Taiwan Strait to honor the shared history of resistance against Japanese aggression and reaffirm calls for national reunification. A symposium in Fuzhou, capital of east China's Fujian Province, brought together about 200 participants, including descendants of Taiwan's anti-Japanese resistance fighters and revolutionary martyrs, young people from both sides of the Strait, representatives from Hong Kong, Macao and overseas communities, and experts and scholars. Song Tao, head of both the Taiwan Work Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council, said at the symposium that the establishment of Taiwan Recovery Day underscored China's firm resolve to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity and helped consolidate the international consensus on upholding the one-China principle. Song urged people on both sides of the Strait to carry forward the spirit of the Chinese people's resistance against Japanese aggression and resolutely oppose "Taiwan independence" secessionism and foreign interference. He pledged firm support for patriots in Taiwan who support reunification and reaffirmed the mainland's commitment to advancing national reunification. Hung Hsiu-chu, former chairwoman of the Chinese Kuomintang party and chairwoman of the Taiwan-based Chinese Cyan Geese Peace Education Foundation, said people on both sides of the Strait should carry forward the spirit of those who defended the country's territory and work toward peaceful reunification. Following its war against China in 1894, Japan seized Taiwan and the Penghu Islands in 1895, subjecting Taiwan to five decades of colonial rule. Taiwan's recovery in 1945 marked a hard-won victory in the Chinese people's resistance against Japanese aggression during World War II and a defining moment in the nation's efforts to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity. In October 2025, China's national legislature designated Oct. 25 as Taiwan Recovery Day. In Beijing, the Central Committee of the Taiwan Democratic Self-Government League held a commemorative event on Saturday at a memorial square in the city's western suburbs. Participants observed a moment of silence, sang songs and laid flowers before a monument measuring 14 meters long and 4 meters high, paying tribute to those who sacrificed their lives for national reunification. Xu Yunchu, granddaughter of revolutionary martyr Zhu Feng, said the history of Taiwan's recovery demonstrated that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China. "Our territory must remain undivided, and our nation must remain united. Chinese on both sides of the Strait should work together to safeguard the common homeland of the Chinese nation," she said. Chen Wen-cheng, a young participant from Taiwan, said establishing Taiwan Recovery Day was significant in strengthening historical awareness among people in Taiwan and deepening emotional ties across the Strait. He called on younger generations to preserve their shared historical memory and carry forward the aspirations of their predecessors. Other commemorative activities included the release in Beijing of a music video about Taiwan's recovery, an exhibition in Shanghai featuring historical materials on Taiwan people's resistance against Japanese aggression, and a seminar in Jinhua, Zhejiang Province, on the history and legacy of the Taiwan volunteer corps, a force formed by patriotic Taiwan residents to resist Japanese aggression during WWII. China Post also issued a commemorative stamp marking Taiwan Recovery Day on Sunday. Featuring the Great Wall, Alishan and Sun Moon Lake, the stamp attracted strong interest from collectors at postal outlets and online platforms across the mainland. In Taiwan, representatives from more than 20 groups gathered on Sunday at the Taipei Zhongshan Hall, where a ceremony to accept Japan's surrender in Taiwan Province of the China war theater of the Allied powers was held in 1945, marking the end of five decades of Japanese colonial rule. Participants sang a song commemorating Taiwan's recovery and paid tribute to those who fought against Japanese aggression before a stone monument in the square outside the hall. The commemorative event took place as the secessionist-minded Democratic Progressive Party authorities in Taiwan have conspicuously avoided mentioning China's victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and China's recovery of Taiwan, and repeatedly downplayed or whitewashed Japan's colonial rule over the island. Hsiung Yi, deputy secretary-general of the Reunification Alliance Party in Taiwan, said Taiwan's recovery is a shared historical memory of all Chinese people. "History must not be forgotten. We must never erase the crimes committed by the aggressors. I hope more people in Taiwan will remember this day and the profound significance it carries," Hsiung said. A Taipei resident surnamed Yu, whose family originated in east China's Shandong Province, said her father had often reminded the family that "we are Chinese." She attended the ceremony because she was concerned about insufficient media coverage of the anniversary and wanted to support efforts to preserve historical truth. Chi Hsing, who works with Taiwan-based magazine The Observer, said the joint commemorations on both sides of the Strait underscored that both sides of the Strait belong to an inseparable community with a shared future. The ceremony concluded with representatives reading a joint statement calling for remembrance of history, opposition to Japanese militarism, the preservation of peace and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. This photo shows commemorative stamps issued by China Post to mark Taiwan Recovery Day. China Post issued a commemorative stamp marking Taiwan Recovery Day on Sunday. Featuring the Great Wall, Alishan and Sun Moon Lake, the stamp attracted strong interest from collectors at postal outlets and online platforms across the mainland. item.title: 20th CPC Central Committee starts fifth plenary session
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
20th CPC Central Committee starts fifth plenary session BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC) started its fifth plenary session in Beijing on Monday morning. Xi Jinping, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, delivered a work report on behalf of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and expounded on a draft decision of the CPC Central Committee on some major issues concerning strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance with perseverance. The draft decision summarizes the achievements and experience of full and rigorous Party self-governance in the new era in a truth-seeking manner, and offers in-depth analysis of the situation and tasks concerning Party building at present and for some time to come. It also sets out strategic plans for strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance with perseverance, according to a Political Bureau meeting in September that decided to submit the document to the plenum for review. Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the full and rigorous Party self-governance has made significant progress, opened up a new frontier for the century-old Party in self-reform, and brought about historic achievements and transformations in the cause of the Party and the country, said an earlier Political Bureau meeting in July that set the plenum's agenda. The meeting said the Party and the people have won the historical initiative to build a strong Party and country, but noted that as profound changes unfold in the world, in China and within the Party, efforts to exercise full and rigorous Party self-governance also face many new circumstances and challenges. It called for adopting higher standards and taking more concrete measures to uphold and apply the valuable experience of full and rigorous Party self-governance in the new era, resolve the prominent issues facing Party building, and consolidate and develop the sound political environment created through Party self-supervision and self-governance. item.title: China brings archaeological sites closer to the public
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
China brings archaeological sites closer to the public People visit the Dahecun site museum in Zhengzhou, central China's Henan Province, June 14, 2025. (Xinhua/Hao Yuan) BEIJING, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- At the Dahecun National Archaeological Site Park in Zhengzhou, central China's Henan Province, reeds sway in the autumn breeze and deer can be heard calling across the nearly 2,400-mu (160-hectare) landscape. The new Dahecun Site Museum within the park is built largely underground, with a sloping entrance leading visitors into the history of a Neolithic settlement dating back about 7,000 years. "This is the country's first thematic museum to present the Yangshao Culture in a panoramic form," said Wang Xiaoya, a guide at the museum. "Its rectangular roof is level with the ground, allowing the building to blend into the landscape like an archaeological site emerging from the soil." Inside, more than 1,500 cultural relics illustrate the Yangshao Culture and shed light on the history of the Dahecun site. Outside, the core protection zone displays the remains of a large Yangshao-period settlement. Offering an important window into a Neolithic culture that lasted about 2,000 years, Dahecun is one of China's major archaeological sites, where protection and public presentation are making the traces of ancient life more accessible to the public. Known in Chinese as "dayizhi," these archaeological sites include the remains of major ancient settlements, cities, palaces and tombs, as well as related groups of sites and cultural landscapes. They carry historical and cultural information across different stages of ancient Chinese history, and are distinguished by their scale, historical and cultural significance, and far-reaching influence. The category includes sites such as Liangzhu in east China's Zhejiang Province, the Yin Ruins in Henan, Sanxingdui in the southwestern province of Sichuan, the Old Summer Palace ruins in Beijing, the Xixia Imperial Tombs and the Great Wall. These sites attest to China's million-year human history, 10,000-year cultural history and more than 5,000-year-old civilization. China now has 150 such archaeological sites. A total of 65 national archaeological site parks have been established based on some of these sites, incorporating the surrounding areas. Luoyang, a city in Henan with 4,000 years of urban history and more than 1,500 years as a capital, is home to several major archaeological sites that are closely woven into the modern cityscape. "Several major archaeological sites lie within an east-west stretch of less than 50 kilometers along the Luo River, including Erlitou, the Yanshi Shang Dynasty Capital Ruins, the Han-Wei Luoyang Ancient City site, the Sui-Tang Luoyang City site and the Mangshan tombs," said Zhao Xiaojun, head of the Luoyang municipal cultural heritage bureau. "The density, scale, time span and richness of historical content are rare in the world." This photo taken on Jan. 29, 2024 shows the details of a turquoise dragon-form artifact at Chinese Archaeological Museum in Beijing, capital of China. (Xinhua/Li He) As early as the 1950s, Luoyang developed a new urban area away from the old city and required archaeological excavations before construction began. Authorities have adopted site-specific regulations to protect these archaeological sites. The Sui-Tang Luoyang City site, the Han-Wei Luoyang Ancient City site and Erlitou have all become national archaeological site parks and cultural landmarks woven into city life. Nationwide, more people are visiting such places. According to statistics, visits to China's national archaeological site parks rose from 20.97 million in 2021 to 97.74 million in 2025, bringing the five-year total to 303 million. Their benefits also extend beyond archaeological research and museum exhibitions. In Zhejiang, efforts to link Liangzhu Culture with rural revitalization have supported local economic development. The operating income of village collectives in 14 villages within the site area rose 19 percent year on year in 2025. At the Liulihe site in Beijing, a China-U.S. international field archaeology summer school offers young people from around the world a platform to learn about Chinese civilization. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for the development of national cultural heritage calls for systematic protection and utilization of such sites. A recent national conference on work related to major archaeological sites stressed the need for high-level archaeological research, sustainable protection and efficient management, while also calling for high-quality presentation. For sites in city centers, small-scale exhibition spaces will be integrated into the urban fabric, while sites in suburban and rural areas can explore models that combine rural revitalization with educational field trips and study programs. Efforts will also be made to improve the cultural services provided by these sites, better realize the value of cultural heritage and meet public needs. For visitors, these sites offer a more direct encounter with the past. Standing among the reeds at Dahecun, they may wonder whether the people who lived here 7,000 years ago saw the same landscape. item.title: 33rd China Yangling Agricultural Hi-tech Fair opens

33rd China Yangling Agricultural Hi-tech Fair opens A visitor learns about a platform of the Internet of Things at the 33rd China Yangling Agricultural Hi-tech Fair in Yangling, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, Oct. 25, 2026. Under the theme of "A New Future of Agriculture with New Quality Productive Forces," the 33rd China Yangling Agricultural Hi-tech Fair opened in Yangling on Sunday, alongside the 2026 Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Agricultural Expo. Covering a total exhibition area of 140,000 square meters, this year's fair features nine exhibition zones showcasing agricultural high-tech achievements, international agricultural cooperation, Shaanxi's modern agriculture and the promotion of practical agricultural technologies, among other areas. item.title: Retracing an odyssey: Why people walk China's Long March 90 years later
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
Retracing an odyssey: Why people walk China's Long March 90 years later BEIJING, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- One man, one horse and more than a year on the road. In 2017, Luo Jianhua set out on horseback from Ruijin in east China to retrace the historic Long March. His wife, Ding Qimei, followed in a support vehicle. Together, they crossed 81 counties and districts across 11 provincial-level regions before reaching Wuqi in northwest China, completing the journey in one year and nine days. In 2024, Luo and Ding took to the road again with their daughter and grandniece, this time tracing the route of the Red Army's West Route Army. Born into a farming family in southwest China's Guizhou Province, Luo grew up hearing stories of the Red Army from his elders. One saying stayed with him: "When life gets tough, think of the Red Army's 12,500-kilometer Long March." A drone photo shows people visiting the revolutionary site of the Battle of Qinggangpo in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, Sept. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Yang Wenbin) Luo left school at 17 to make a living, later running businesses ranging from a coal-washing plant and a pig farm to an organic rice cultivation company. While the stories he had heard as a child sustained him through difficult times, Luo long harbored a desire to experience firsthand what the Red Army had endured. STEPPING INTO HISTORY Hailed by American journalist Edgar Snow as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times," the Long March took place at a time when China was beset by foreign aggression, social turmoil and destitution. Facing encirclement by overwhelming and much better-armed Kuomintang forces, the Communist Party of China (CPC)-led Red Army embarked on the epic military trek from 1934 to 1936. During the march, the troops crossed nearly 100 rivers, traversed vast grasslands once known as a "death trap," and climbed over more than 40 mountains, including more than 20 snow-capped mountains rising above 4,000 meters. This military maneuver gave the CPC a new foothold in northwest China, from which it built up its strength, fought back against invading Japanese troops and eventually toppled the corrupt Kuomintang regime, leading to the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949. An aerial drone photo taken on Aug. 11, 2026 shows a view of the Caiwan Town of Quanzhou County of Guilin City, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Huang Xiaobang) For Luo, retracing the route made the Red Army's hardships that he had read about far more tangible. In northwest Sichuan Province, he and his horse once sank into a marsh. As he struggled to free the animal, he thought about the soldiers who had crossed similar terrain decades earlier. "I felt for them. They had so little food and equipment, yet they had to keep going through wind and hail. Some fell and never got up again," he said. Luo is not alone. People from China and abroad continue to retrace the Long March, some covering the entire route and others exploring sections by car or on foot. For many, the journey offers a way to learn about the Red Army's history, understand the CPC and see how China has changed over the decades. The Long March's reach has extended beyond China. First published in Britain in 1937, Snow's "Red Star Over China" introduced the Chinese revolution to international readers. Decades later, Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Harrison Salisbury retraced the route and described the Long March as "a great human epic." That appeal continues today. Dutch sinologist Elsbeth van Paridon, who joined a group retracing the route this summer, said walking the route gave her a feeling similar to looking out over the beaches of Normandy and realizing what had happened there. She noted that the former revolutionary sites along the route now also serve as ecological parks, becoming part of a broader tourism economy that supports local development. "That is how you see the spirit of the Long March live on," she said. This photo taken with a mobile phone shows William N. Brown, a U.S. professor at Xiamen University, taking photos in Qinggangpo Village of Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, June 28, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Si) William N. Brown, a U.S. professor at Xiamen University who has lived in China for nearly 40 years, has retraced part of the route and witnessed the country's transformation firsthand. He first traveled to Guizhou in 1994, when unpaved roads and limited river crossings left mountain communities isolated. Pointing to a towering bridge spanning a valley in Qinggangpo Village, Brown highlighted the region's staggering leap in connectivity. "The most important change is invisible: people have gained confidence and self-respect," he said. "Thirty years ago, many thought prosperity would take 50 years to achieve -- they never expected to see it in their own lifetime." THE SAME ROAD, A TRANSFORMED CHINA The changes are also visible in the country's infrastructure. Roads now cut through mountains that Red Army soldiers once crossed on foot, while bridges span valleys and rivers that once posed major obstacles. China's operational high-speed rail network has surpassed 50,000 kilometers, accounting for over 70 percent of the world's total. Its expressway network extends to nearly 200,000 kilometers, the largest in the world. An aerial drone photo taken on July 31, 2026 shows the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge in southwest China's Guizhou Province. (Xinhua) The transformation is particularly visible in Guizhou, where rugged karst terrain long made travel difficult. More than 32,000 bridges have been completed or are under construction in the province, including the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge, the world's highest bridge. Communities along the historic route have also changed. In Guangxi's Quanzhou, Guanyang and Xing'an counties, where the Battle of the Xiangjiang River was fought, more than 100 formerly impoverished villages have been lifted out of poverty through targeted poverty alleviation efforts. Despite China's profound transformation over recent decades, new challenges remain on its path toward Chinese modernization. Wan Laizhi, a scholar of CPC history at Guangxi Normal University, said retracing the Long March route helps people appreciate how earlier generations faced adversity and held to their convictions, drawing strength and inspiration from their example to overcome challenges facing China today. Chen Lipeng, a professor at Renmin University of China, said retracing the route can also help promote tourism in former revolutionary areas and support rural revitalization. Tourists visit the historical site of the Zunyi Meeting in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Tian Jinhong/Xinhua) Interest in revolutionary heritage sites is growing, particularly among younger visitors. In the first half of 2026, interest in booking tickets for such attractions rose 86 percent year on year, while bookings by people aged 18 to 35 accounted for more than half of the total, according to industry data. Luo and Ding, for their part, have worked to keep that history alive. Back home in Zunyi City, they compiled their experiences into books and began visiting schools to share what they had learned. Earlier this year, they opened a homestay in their village, employing more than 10 local residents. Luo plans to turn part of it into a small educational site displaying materials collected during their journeys. "Young people today may not face the hardships people endured in the past, but everyone encounters difficulties in life," he said. "I want them to know that there is always a way forward. That is what the Long March spirit means to me." Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.
